Unit 4: Topics 1,2,3,4

Cell Communication
Cell-to-cell communication is critical for the function
and survival of cells
● Responsible for the growth and development of
  multicellular organisms

How Do Cells Communicate?
Cells communicate through three general ways
       1. Direct Contact
       2. Local Signaling
       3. Long-distance signaling

Direct Contact
● Direct contact: communication through cell junctions
  ○ Signaling substances and other material dissolved in
     the cytoplasm can pass freely between adjacent
     cells
      ■ Animal cells: gap junctions
      ■ Plant cells: plasmodesmata

● Animals and plants use hormones for long

  ○ Animals use endocrine signaling

Quick Review
1. What are the three stages of cell signaling?
    a. Answer: reception, transduction, reponse
2. What is the actual “signal” being transduced in a
   signal transduction pathway?
    a. Answer: a ligand
3. How is this “signal” passed from outside to inside
   the cell?
    a. Answer: through transduction. During
       transduction the signal is relayed by protein
       kinases and amplified by second messengers

Signal Transduction Pathways
● Signal transduction pathways can influence how
  a cell responds to its environment
  ○ They can result in changes in gene expression
     and cell function
     ■ Can alter phenotypes or result in cell death

Changes in Signal Transduction
             Pathways
● Mutations to receptor proteins or to any
  component of the signaling pathway will result in
  a change to the transduction of the signal

AP BIOLOGY
Unit 4: Topic 5

Overview
The body must be able to monitor its internal
conditions at all times
● Set points: values for various physiological
  conditions that the body tries to maintain
   ○ This set point has a normal range for which it can
     fluctuate
      ■ Example: body temperature
         ● Set point: 98.6℉
         ● Normal range: 97℉ to 99℉

Overview
Homeostasis: the state of relatively stable internal
conditions
● Organisms detect and respond to a stimulus
● Think: balance
● The body maintains homeostasis through
  feedback loops

Feedback loops
There are two types of feedback loops: negative and
positive
Terms to know:
Stimulus: a variable that will cause a response
Receptor/sensor: sensory organs that detect a
stimulus. This information is sent to the control
center (brain)
Effector: muscle or gland that will respond
Response: changes (decreases or increases) the
effect of the stimulus

Negative Feedback
● The most common feedback mechanism
● This type of feedback reduces the effect of the
  stimulus
  ○ Examples:
     ■ Sweat
     ■ Blood sugar
     ■ Breathing rate

Example: Negative Feedback
                         Body temperature regulation
   Stimulus: heat                                                             Stimulus: cold



Receptor: temperature                                                  Receptor: temperature
receptors in skin                                                      receptors in skin



Effector: sweat glands                    Happy Patrick                       Effector: muscles



  Response: sweat                                                                  Response:
                                                                                   shivering



                         Sweaty Patrick                   Shivering Patrick

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Positive Feedback
● This type of feedback increases the effect of a
  stimulus
  ○ Examples:
     ■ Child labor
     ■ Blood clotting
     ■ Fruit ripening

                                     Childbirth

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Homeostatic Imbalances
There are many reasons for why the body may not
be able to regulate homeostasis
● For example:
   ○ Genetic disorders
   ○ Drug or alcohol abuse
   ○ Intolerable conditions (ie extreme heat or cold)

Homeostatic Imbalances
Disease: when the body is unable to maintain
homeostasis
● Examples:
   ○ Cancer: the body cannot regulate cell growth
   ○ Diabetes: the body cannot regulate blood glucose
     levels

Cell Signaling as a Means of Homeostasis
● In order to maintain homeostasis, the cells in a
  multicellular organism must be able to
  communicate
● Communication occurs through signal
  transduction pathways

AP BIOLOGY
Unit 4: Topics 6 & 7

Cell Cycle
● The cell division process is an integral part of life
   ○ Allows for the reproduction of cells, growth of
      cells, and tissue repair
● Cell cycle: the life of a cell from its formation until
  it divides

Organization of DNA
Cells must organize and package their DNA before
division
● DNA associates with and wraps around proteins
   known as histones to form nucleosomes
    ○ Strings of nucleosomes form chromatin
     ■ When a cell is not actively dividing, chromatin is
       in a non-condensed form
     ■ After DNA replication, chromatin condenses to
       form a chromosome
        ● Chromosomes are densely packed to allow
           for easier division

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:

Since the DNA was replicated, each chromosome has a
duplicated copy         ● The copies join together to form
                          sister chromatids
                              ○ Centromere: the region on
                                each sister chromatid where
                                they are most closely
                                attached
                              ○ Kinetochore: proteins
                                attached to the centromere
                                that link each sister
                                chromatid to the mitotic
                                spindle

Genome
Genome: all of a cell’s genetic information (DNA)
● Prokaryotes: singular, circular DNA
● Eukaryotes: one or more linear chromosomes
  ○ Every eukaryote has a specific number of
     chromosomes
      ■ Humans: 46
      ■ Chimps: 48
      ■ Elephants: 56

Genome
● Homologous chromosomes: two chromosomes
  (one from mom and one from dad) that are the
  same length, have the same centromere position,
  and carry genes controlling the same
  characteristics

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Cell Cycle
● The cell cycle consists of alternating phases of
  interphase and mitosis
   ○ G1→ S→ G2 → mitosis → cytokinesis

      Interphase

Cell Cycle
Interphase
 ● The longest portion of the cell cycle (90%)
    ○ G1 “first gap” phase
      ■ The cell grows and carries out normal functions
   ○ S “synthesis” phase
      ■ DNA replication and chromosome duplication
        occurs
   ○ G2 “second gap” phase
      ■ Final growth and preparation for mitosis
M Phase
● Mitosis: nucleus divides
● Cytokinesis: cytoplasm divides
● Mitosis results in 2 identical diploid daughter cells

Phases of Mitosis
Mitosis is broken down into 5 stages:
1. Prophase
2. Prometaphase
3. Metaphase
4. Anaphase
5. Telophase and cytokinesis
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Five-stage mitosis sequence includes prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase/cytokinesis.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prophase
Key events:
● Chromatin condenses
● Nucleoli disappear
● Duplicated
  chromosomes appear
  as sister chromatids
● Mitotic spindle begins to
  form
● Centrosomes move
  away from each other
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Prophase cell diagram shows condensing chromosomes and separating centrosomes.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prometaphase
Key events:
● Nuclear envelope
  fragments
● Microtubules enter
  nuclear area and
  some attach to
  kinetochores
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Prometaphase diagram shows nuclear-envelope breakdown and spindle microtubules entering the former nuclear region.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Metaphase
Key events:
● Centrosomes are at
  opposite poles
● Chromosomes line up
  at the metaphase
  plate
● Microtubules are
  attached to each
  kinetochore
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Metaphase diagram shows chromosomes aligned at the metaphase plate with kinetochore attachments.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Anaphase
Key events:
● Sister chromatids
  separate and move
  to opposite ends of
  the cell due to the
  microtubules
  shortening
● Cell elongates
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Anaphase diagram shows sister chromatids moving apart while the cell elongates.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Telophase and Cytokinesis
Key events:
● Two daughter nuclei
  form
● Nucleoli reappear
● Chromosomes
  become less
  condensed

     travel to the middle of
     the cell and form a
     cell plate

Regulation of the Cell Cycle
● Throughout the cell cycle there are checkpoints
  ○ Control points that regulate the cell cycle
    ■ Cells receive stop/go signals

Major Checkpoints
G1 Checkpoint
● Most important checkpoint
● Checks for cell size, growth
   factors, and DNA damage
● Stop/Go signals
    ○ “Go”- cell completes the
      whole cell cycle
    ○ “Stop”- cell enters a
      nondividing (quiescent)
      state known as G0
      phase
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: G1 checkpoint diagram places a stop/go control before S phase and shows possible entry to G0.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Major Checkpoints
G0
● Some cells stay in G0
  forever (muscle/nerve
  cells)
● Some cells can be called
  back into the cell cycle
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: G0 diagram shows an exit from the cycling path.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Major Checkpoints
G2 Checkpoint
● Checks for completion of DNA
   replication and DNA damage
● “Go”--cell proceeds to mitosis
● “Stop”-- cell cycle stops and
   the cell will attempt to repair
   damage
   ○ If damage cannot be repaired
     the cell will undergo apoptosis
      ■ Programmed cell death
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: G2 checkpoint diagram places stop/go control before mitosis and connects irreparable damage to apoptosis.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Major Checkpoints
M (Spindle) Checkpoint
● Checks for microtubule
   attachment to chromosomes at
   the kinetochores at metaphase
● “Go”--cell proceeds to
   anaphase and completes
   mitosis
● “Stop”-- cell will pause mitosis
   to allow for spindles to finish
   attaching to chromosomes
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: M/spindle checkpoint diagram places control at metaphase before anaphase.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Internal Cell Cycle Regulators
● Regulation of the cell cycle involves an internal
  control system that consists of:
1. Proteins known as cyclins
   ○ Concentration of cyclins varies
      ■ Cyclins are synthesized and degraded at specific
        stages of the cell cycle
2. Enzymes known as cyclin-dependent kinases
   (CDKs)
   ○ Concentration remains constant through each
     phase of the cell cycle
      ■ Active only when its specific cyclin is present
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Cell-cycle diagram and text contrast oscillating cyclin concentration with relatively stable CDK abundance.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Internal Cell Cycle Regulators
 ● Each cyclin-CDK complex has a specific regulatory
   effect
   ○ Active CDK complexes phosphorylate target
      proteins, which help regulate key events in the
      cell cycle


Notice: varying
levels of different
cyclins in each
stage
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Graph shows phase-specific cyclin concentration curves across G1, S, G2, and mitosis.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
External Cell Cycle Regulators
● Growth factors: hormones released by cells that
  stimulate cell growth
   ○ Signal transduction pathway is initiated
     ■ CDKs are activated leading to progression
        through the cell cycle
● Contact (or density) inhibition: Cell surface
  receptors recognize contact with other cells
   ○ Initiates signal transduction pathway that stops the
     cell cycle in G1 phase
● Anchorage dependence: cells rely on attachment
  to other cells or the extracellular matrix to divide

Cancer: Evasion of the Cell Cycle
● Normal cells become cancerous through DNA
  mutations
  ○ DNA mutations: changes in the DNA
    ■ Cancer cells on average have accumulated 60
      or more mutations on genes that regulate cell
      growth
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Tumor diagram contrasts a growing mass of cancer cells with neighboring normal tissue.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Normal Cells vs Cancer Cells
     Normal Cells             Cancer Cells

● Follow checkpoints      ● Do not follow
● Divide on average         checkpoints
  20-50 times in          ● Divide infinitely when
  culture (in petri         in culture
  dishes)                    ○ Considered to be
● Go through                   “immortal”
  apoptosis when          ● Evade apoptosis and
  there are significant     continue dividing
  errors                    even with errors
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Two-column comparison contrasts checkpoint behavior, finite culture division, apoptosis, and cancer-cell properties.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Cancer Cells
● The uncontrollable growth of cancer cells can lead
  to a tumor
   ○ A mass of tissue formed by abnormal cells
     ■ Benign tumor: cells are abnormal, but not
       considered to be cancerous (yet)
        ● Cells remain at only the tumor site and are
          unable to spread elsewhere in the body
     ■ Malignant tumor: mass of cancerous cells that
       lose their anchorage dependency and can leave
       the tumor site
        ● Metastasis: when cells separate from the
          tumor and spread elsewhere in the body

Cancer Prevention
 ● Unfortunately, cancer can affect anyone. However, there
    are various things that you can do that will minimize your
    risk of developing cancer:
     ○ Do not smoke (cigarettes, vape products)
        ■ Nicotine causes mutations in cells at high rates
     ○ Eat healthy and drink water
        ■ Fatty foods and dehydration can affect the functions
            of cells
     ○ Protect your skin from the sun by using SPF
        ■ Sun is damaging to skin cells and can cause
            mutations to occur after exposure
If possible, ask your family about any history of cancer and
receive regular cancer screenings

Practice FRQ
Vinblastine is a chemotherapeutic drug often administered to
patients suffering from Hodgkin’s lymphoma, lung cancer, and
bladder cancer. Vinblastine works by entering cancer cells and
binding to tubulin, which is a protein that forms microtubules.
Once Vinblastine has bound to tubulin, it inhibits the assembly of
microtubules and proper formation of the mitotic spindle. This
causes the cell cycle to arrest. a) Identify and explain two
phases of the cell cycle most affected by Vinblastine. b) Identify
the checkpoint that is most likely responsible for arresting the
cell cycle.
a)Metaphase: microtubule attachment to the kinetochore would not happen
Anaphase: since microtubule attachment did not occur, the sister chromatids
would not separate
b) M (spindle) checkpoint

ced_current_atoms.label: Direct or distance communication
ced_current_atoms.statement: Cells communicate with one another through direct contact with other cells or from a distance via chemical signaling.

ced_current_atoms.label: Short-distance local regulators
ced_current_atoms.statement: Cells communicate over short distances by using local regulators that target cells in the vicinity of the signal-emitting cell.

ced_current_atoms.label: Long-distance signaling
ced_current_atoms.statement: Signals released by one cell type can travel long distances to target cells of another type.

ced_current_atoms.label: Signal pathway links reception to response
ced_current_atoms.statement: Signal transduction pathways link signal reception with cellular responses.

ced_current_atoms.label: Protein modification and phosphorylation cascades
ced_current_atoms.statement: Many signal transduction pathways include protein modifications and involve phosphorylation cascades.

ced_current_atoms.label: Ligand recognition by receptor
ced_current_atoms.statement: Signaling begins when a chemical messenger, a ligand, is recognized by a receptor protein in a target cell.

ced_current_atoms.label: Ligand-binding specificity
ced_current_atoms.statement: A receptor ligand-binding domain recognizes a specific chemical messenger, which may be a peptide/protein or a small molecule.

ced_current_atoms.label: GPCR example
ced_current_atoms.statement: G protein-coupled receptors are an example of receptor proteins in eukaryotes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Receptor location
ced_current_atoms.statement: Receptors may be located on the surface of a target cell or in the cytoplasm or nucleus of the target cell.

ced_current_atoms.label: Relay, amplification, and response
ced_current_atoms.statement: Signaling cascades relay signals from receptors to cellular targets, often amplifying incoming signals and producing responses such as cell growth, secretion, or gene expression.

ced_current_atoms.label: Ligand-induced receptor shape change
ced_current_atoms.statement: After ligand binding, the intracellular domain or state of a receptor changes, initiating signal transduction.

ced_current_atoms.label: Enzymes and second messengers
ced_current_atoms.statement: Enzymes and second messengers such as cyclic AMP (cAMP) relay and amplify intracellular signals.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hormones as long-distance messengers
ced_current_atoms.statement: Hormones are signaling messengers that can travel long distances, including through the bloodstream in animals.

ced_current_atoms.label: Ligand-gated channels
ced_current_atoms.statement: Ligand binding to ligand-gated channels can cause the channel to open or close.

ced_current_atoms.label: Signal response changes phenotype/function
ced_current_atoms.statement: Signal transduction can change gene expression and cell function, alter phenotype, or contribute to programmed cell death (apoptosis).

ced_current_atoms.label: Mutations alter signaling
ced_current_atoms.statement: Changes in receptor domains or other signaling-pathway components can alter downstream signal transduction and cellular responses.

ced_current_atoms.label: Chemicals activate or inhibit pathways
ced_current_atoms.statement: Chemicals that interact with signaling-pathway components may activate or inhibit the pathway.

ced_current_atoms.label: Feedback maintains internal environment
ced_current_atoms.statement: Organisms use feedback mechanisms to maintain internal environments in response to internal and external changes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Negative feedback
ced_current_atoms.statement: Negative feedback reduces the initial stimulus and helps return a perturbed system toward a regulated target or set point at molecular, cellular, or organismal levels.

ced_current_atoms.label: Positive feedback
ced_current_atoms.statement: Positive feedback amplifies a response so the initiating variable is driven further in the same direction until another event ends the loop.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cell cycle regulation
ced_current_atoms.statement: The cell cycle is a highly regulated series of events controlling growth and reproduction of eukaryotic cells.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cell-cycle stages
ced_current_atoms.statement: The cell cycle includes sequential stages of interphase (G1, S, G2), mitosis, and cytokinesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: G1 phase
ced_current_atoms.statement: During G1, the cell is metabolically active and duplicates organelles and cytosolic components as it grows.

ced_current_atoms.label: S phase
ced_current_atoms.statement: During S phase, DNA replicates so each replicated chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere.

ced_current_atoms.label: G2 phase
ced_current_atoms.statement: During G2, the cell continues protein synthesis and preparation for mitosis; centrosome duplication is completed by this period in typical animal cells.

ced_current_atoms.label: G0 stage and reentry
ced_current_atoms.statement: A cell may enter a nondividing G0 state and some cell types can reenter the cell cycle in response to appropriate cues.

ced_current_atoms.label: Nondividing cells
ced_current_atoms.statement: Nondividing cells may exit the cell cycle or remain held in a nondividing state.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mitosis genome transmission
ced_current_atoms.statement: Mitosis segregates replicated chromosomes so daughter nuclei receive complete, equivalent genome sets, barring mutation or segregation error.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mitosis roles
ced_current_atoms.statement: Mitosis contributes to growth, tissue repair, and asexual reproduction in eukaryotes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mitosis sequence
ced_current_atoms.statement: The AP framework organizes mitosis into prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase, alternating with interphase in the cell cycle.

ced_current_atoms.label: Prophase
ced_current_atoms.statement: In prophase, replicated chromosomes condense, the mitotic spindle begins forming, and centrosomes move toward opposite poles.

ced_current_atoms.label: Metaphase
ced_current_atoms.statement: In metaphase, spindle microtubules position chromosomes at the cell equator/metaphase plate.

ced_current_atoms.label: Anaphase
ced_current_atoms.statement: In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles as spindle dynamics redistribute the chromosomes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Telophase
ced_current_atoms.statement: In telophase, the mitotic spindle disassembles, new nuclear envelopes form, and chromosomes begin to decondense.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cytokinesis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm; animal cells typically form a cleavage furrow and plant cells form a cell plate, producing two daughter cells.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cell-cycle checkpoints
ced_current_atoms.statement: Internal controls and checkpoints regulate progression through the cell cycle.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cyclin-CDK control
ced_current_atoms.statement: Interactions between cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) regulate progression through the cell cycle.

ced_current_atoms.label: Disrupted cell-cycle control
ced_current_atoms.statement: Disruptions to cell-cycle regulation can contribute to cancer or trigger apoptosis (programmed cell death).

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The slide says dissolved signaling substances and other cytoplasmic material can pass “freely” through gap junctions/plasmodesmata.
review_flags.resolution: Intercellular junctions permit passage of selected small molecules/ions or cytoplasmic continuity, but transport is constrained and can be regulated; do not encode unrestricted passage.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Paracrine signaling is defined as acting on an “adjacent” cell.
review_flags.resolution: Paracrine signals act locally on nearby target cells; direct membrane adjacency is not required.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Plant hormones are presented as generally traveling in xylem/phloem or through air.
review_flags.resolution: Plant hormones can move through tissues/vascular routes; volatile ethylene can diffuse through air. Airborne travel is a special case, not a universal plant-hormone route.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The slide says all receptors have an area that transmits a signal to another protein.
review_flags.resolution: Receptors have ligand-binding regions and produce intracellular effects, but not every receptor signals by handing a signal to another protein; ligand-gated channels and intracellular receptors work differently.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck presents membrane-receptor categories and ligand-property rules more broadly than the current CED requires.
review_flags.resolution: Keep receptor-location logic and GPCR/ligand-gated-channel examples; detailed receptor taxonomy remains teacher enrichment unless explicitly required.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Membrane receptors are described as binding ligands that are polar/water-soluble/large, implying a strict rule.
review_flags.resolution: Hydrophilic or sufficiently large ligands generally require cell-surface receptors because they do not readily cross the lipid bilayer; treat this as a membrane-permeability principle, not an absolute classification shortcut.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Steroid, thyroid hormone, and nitric oxide intracellular signaling examples are included.
review_flags.resolution: Scientifically retain as teacher enrichment. The CED requires receptor location but does not require memorizing these example classes.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Quick Review calls the ligand “the actual signal being transduced.”
review_flags.resolution: The ligand carries the extracellular message and binds the receptor; usually the ligand itself is not passed through the intracellular cascade. Signal transduction relays information through receptor and downstream molecular state changes.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Protein phosphatase is described as shutting off pathways.
review_flags.resolution: Protein phosphatases remove phosphate groups. Dephosphorylation can inactivate or activate a target depending on the protein and pathway; avoid a universal “phosphatase = off” rule.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Phosphorylation is framed mainly as a relay/activation step.
review_flags.resolution: Protein kinases transfer phosphate groups and phosphorylation changes protein state/activity; phosphorylation can activate or inhibit depending on the target.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck states there are two main categories of eukaryotic cell-membrane receptors: GPCRs and ion channels.
review_flags.resolution: Those are two important receptor types, not an exhaustive pair; receptor tyrosine kinases and other membrane receptors also exist. Preserve GPCR and ligand-gated channels as teacher/CED examples without encoding a false exhaustive taxonomy.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: GTP is described as an energy molecule similar to ATP.
review_flags.resolution: In heterotrimeric G-protein signaling, GDP/GTP binding acts primarily as a molecular switch; GTP hydrolysis helps terminate the active state. Do not teach GTP’s role here mainly as energy supply.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Feedback-loop sensor/control-center language is written as sensory organ → brain → muscle/gland.
review_flags.resolution: That architecture fits some organism-level loops, but feedback also operates at molecular and cellular levels. Generalize sensor/controller/effector roles beyond nervous-system anatomy.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: 98.6°F is presented as a single body-temperature set point with a fixed normal range.
review_flags.resolution: Human core temperature varies with time, site, activity, hormones, and individuals; use dynamic regulated range/set-point language, not a universal exact value.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Disease is defined as when the body is unable to maintain homeostasis.
review_flags.resolution: Loss of homeostatic regulation can contribute to disease, but disease is broader and should not be defined solely as homeostasis failure.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The slide implies chromosomes form only after DNA replication when chromatin condenses.
review_flags.resolution: A chromosome is a DNA molecule with associated proteins throughout the cell cycle; after S phase each replicated chromosome consists of two sister chromatids, and chromatin becomes highly condensed/visibly distinct during mitosis.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Centromere is described as a region “on each sister chromatid where they are most closely attached.”
review_flags.resolution: The centromere is the specialized chromosome region where sister chromatids are joined and where kinetochore complexes assemble.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Prokaryotes are stated to have singular, circular DNA.
review_flags.resolution: Many bacteria and archaea have a main circular chromosome, but exceptions include multiple chromosomes and linear chromosomes. Keep the common introductory pattern qualified.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Homologous chromosomes are described as carrying genes controlling the same characteristics.
review_flags.resolution: Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding gene loci in the same order but may contain different alleles.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The gamete column says gametes divide by meiosis.
review_flags.resolution: Meiosis occurs in germ-line precursor cells and produces haploid cells/gametes; mature gametes are products of meiosis, not cells that divide by meiosis.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Interphase is stated to be 90% of the cell cycle.
review_flags.resolution: Interphase is often the longest portion of the cycle, but the fraction varies by cell type and conditions; do not encode 90% as universal.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Mitosis is stated to result in two identical diploid daughter cells.
review_flags.resolution: Mitosis is nuclear division that segregates duplicated chromosomes. Mitosis plus cytokinesis usually yields two daughter cells with equivalent chromosome sets to the parent nucleus, barring errors; daughter cells are not necessarily diploid if the parent cell was haploid.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Prometaphase is taught as a separate fifth mitotic stage.
review_flags.resolution: Prometaphase is scientifically valid teacher enrichment. The current CED lists prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase, so separate prometaphase naming is not AP-required recall.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Chromosome poleward movement is attributed to microtubule shortening alone.
review_flags.resolution: Kinetochore microtubule shortening contributes to chromosome movement, while spindle dynamics and motor proteins also contribute; cell elongation involves nonkinetochore spindle microtubules.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: G1 is labeled the “most important checkpoint.”
review_flags.resolution: G1/restriction control is a major decision point, but importance is context-dependent; AP requires checkpoint regulation without ranking one as universally most important.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Muscle and nerve cells are said to stay in G0 forever.
review_flags.resolution: Many terminally differentiated cells, especially most neurons and skeletal muscle fibers, remain nondividing for long periods; some cell types in G0 can reenter the cycle. Avoid absolute “forever” language.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Irreparable G2 damage is shown as deterministically leading to apoptosis.
review_flags.resolution: Persistent DNA damage can trigger arrest, senescence, apoptosis, or other outcomes depending on cell type and signaling context; apoptosis is one important outcome.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Specific cyclin-CDK timing/pairs are shown in teacher material.
review_flags.resolution: The current CED requires the interaction of cyclins and CDKs but explicitly excludes memorization of specific cyclin-CDK pairs and growth factors from AP Exam scope.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Growth factors are defined as hormones released by cells that stimulate growth.
review_flags.resolution: Growth factors are extracellular signaling molecules, often proteins/polypeptides, that can stimulate proliferation or other responses; many act locally and should not be universally classified as hormones.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Density-dependent inhibition and anchorage dependence are taught as external cell-cycle regulators.
review_flags.resolution: Scientifically retain as teacher enrichment supported by Campbell. They are not explicit current-CED required terms.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck says cancer cells average 60 or more mutations in genes regulating cell growth.
review_flags.resolution: Cancer genomes vary enormously by cancer type and individual tumor. Remove the unsupported universal numerical threshold and teach accumulation of driver and passenger alterations without a fixed count.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Cancer cells are presented as universally dividing infinitely and being “immortal.”
review_flags.resolution: Some cancer-derived cells acquire replicative immortality, especially in culture, but not every cancer cell divides indefinitely. Treat immortality as a common hallmark/property of transformed cell populations, not a universal behavior of every cancer cell.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: A benign tumor is described as “not considered cancerous (yet).”
review_flags.resolution: A benign tumor is nonmalignant and localized; it is not defined as a precancerous stage that will later become cancer.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Malignancy is defined mainly by loss of anchorage dependence.
review_flags.resolution: Malignant tumors are cancerous and capable of invading surrounding tissue and, in many cases, metastasizing. Loss of anchorage dependence can contribute but is not the definition of malignancy.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The slide states nicotine causes mutations in cells at high rates.
review_flags.resolution: Nicotine is the primary addictive chemical in tobacco products, while many carcinogens in tobacco smoke and some aerosol exposures cause DNA damage/mutations. Do not teach nicotine itself as the main mutagenic carcinogen.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The slide implies fatty foods and dehydration are direct cancer-prevention mechanisms because they affect cell function.
review_flags.resolution: Remove this unsupported mechanism. Cancer-risk guidance should focus on established evidence-based risk factors; hydration is not a general cancer-prevention mechanism.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Sun exposure is described generically as causing mutations.
review_flags.resolution: Ultraviolet radiation can damage DNA and increase skin-cancer risk; preserve the mechanism as UV-induced DNA damage, not vague sunlight exposure.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The vinblastine FRQ asks for two phases most affected and gives metaphase and anaphase.
review_flags.resolution: Microtubule assembly inhibition disrupts spindle formation/kinetochore attachment in prometaphase/metaphase and normally activates the spindle checkpoint before anaphase. Anaphase is prevented downstream rather than necessarily entered and directly disrupted.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Legacy slide dividers label Unit 4 as Topics 1–4, Topic 5, and Topics 6–7.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve legacy headings as teacher-source metadata. Current AP Unit 4 has Topics 4.1–4.6 and controls AP scope.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Cell-to-cell communication coordinates survival, growth, development, and other multicellular functions.
Direct-contact signaling occurs when cells communicate through cell junctions or direct interactions between cell-surface molecules.
Gap junctions are intercellular channels in animals that permit regulated passage of ions and small signaling molecules between adjacent cells.
Plasmodesmata are membrane-lined channels through plant cell walls that connect cytoplasm of neighboring cells and allow regulated intercellular transport/signaling.
Direct cell-surface interactions between antigen-presenting cells and T cells are an illustrative example of contact-dependent communication.
Local signaling uses secreted chemical messengers that act over short distances on nearby target cells.
A local regulator is a secreted signaling molecule that acts on cells in the vicinity of the signaling cell.
A ligand is a signaling molecule that binds specifically to a receptor and can initiate a signaling response.
A target cell responds to a signaling molecule because it has the appropriate receptor and downstream machinery.
Paracrine signaling is local signaling in which secreted regulators act on nearby target cells.
Growth factors are extracellular signaling molecules that can stimulate nearby target cells to grow, divide, survive, or differentiate depending on context.
Synaptic signaling is specialized local signaling in which a neuron releases neurotransmitter across a narrow synaptic cleft to a target cell.
A neurotransmitter is a chemical signal released by a neuron that diffuses across a synaptic cleft and binds receptors on a target cell.
The synaptic cleft is the narrow extracellular gap between a presynaptic neuron and its target cell across which neurotransmitters diffuse.
Long-distance signaling uses messengers that travel from signaling cells to distant target cells.
A hormone is a signaling molecule produced by cells and transported to target cells, often over long distances.
In animal endocrine signaling, specialized cells release hormones into circulation, allowing them to reach distant target cells.
Plant hormones can move through tissues and vascular pathways; volatile ethylene can also diffuse through air to target tissues.
Insulin is a protein hormone released by pancreatic beta cells in response to elevated blood glucose and acts on target cells with insulin receptors.
Reception is a target cell’s detection of a signaling molecule when the ligand binds its receptor.
A receptor is a macromolecule, usually a protein, whose ligand-binding site recognizes particular signaling molecules and whose activation produces an intracellular effect.
Ligand-receptor binding depends on complementary chemical and structural properties, so only cells with suitable receptors respond directly to a given ligand.
Ligand binding changes receptor conformation or functional state, enabling the receptor to initiate downstream signaling.
Cell-surface receptors span or associate with the plasma membrane and are used by signaling molecules that do not readily cross the lipid bilayer.
Intracellular receptors are located in the cytoplasm or nucleus and bind signaling molecules able to cross the plasma membrane.

Hydrophobic or sufficiently small signaling molecules can cross the lipid bilayer and may bind intracellular receptors; this is a permeability principle, not an AP memorization rule for arbitrary molecules.
Many steroid hormones diffuse through the plasma membrane and bind intracellular receptors that can influence gene expression.
Thyroid hormones are lipid-soluble signaling molecules that bind intracellular nuclear receptors.
Nitric oxide is a small gaseous signaling molecule that can diffuse across membranes and activate intracellular targets such as soluble guanylyl cyclase.
Signal transduction converts information from receptor activation into intracellular molecular changes that can produce a cellular response.
A signal transduction pathway is a sequence of interacting molecular components that relays information from an activated receptor to cellular targets.
A protein kinase transfers a phosphate group, usually from ATP, to a target protein; phosphorylation changes the target protein’s functional state.
A phosphorylation cascade is a series in which activated protein kinases phosphorylate downstream proteins, allowing relay and often amplification of a signal.
A protein phosphatase removes phosphate groups from target proteins and thereby changes their activity or signaling state.
Dephosphorylation is removal of a phosphate group; it may activate or inactivate a target depending on the pathway.
Signal amplification occurs when activation of one signaling component leads to activation of many downstream molecules, increasing the magnitude of the intracellular response.
A second messenger is a small intracellular molecule or ion that relays information from an activated receptor or upstream signaling component to downstream targets.
Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) is a common second messenger that can relay and amplify intracellular signaling.
A cellular response is the change in cell activity produced by a signaling pathway, such as altered membrane transport, enzyme activity, secretion, growth, or gene expression.
Signaling pathways can change membrane permeability by modifying channels or transport proteins.
Signaling pathways can alter metabolic activity by modifying enzymes or other metabolic regulators.
Signaling pathways can activate or repress proteins that regulate transcription and therefore change gene expression.
A GPCR is a cell-surface receptor that changes conformation upon ligand binding and regulates a heterotrimeric G protein on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane.
A heterotrimeric G protein is a membrane-associated molecular switch regulated by GDP/GTP binding and interaction with an activated GPCR.
Activated GPCR promotes release of GDP from the G protein and binding of GTP; the GTP-bound form can regulate downstream effector proteins.
Intrinsic GTPase activity converts GTP to GDP and helps return the G protein to its inactive state; GTP functions here primarily as part of a molecular switch.
An activated G-protein subunit can interact with an effector enzyme or channel, altering downstream signaling and potentially amplifying the response.
A ligand-gated ion channel is a membrane receptor/channel whose open probability changes when a ligand binds, allowing or restricting specific ion movement.
Opening or closing a ligand-gated ion channel changes ion flux and membrane properties, which can initiate downstream cellular responses.
Because signaling can alter gene expression and cellular function, sustained pathway changes can alter phenotype.
Programmed cell death (apoptosis) can be triggered by signaling pathways in response to developmental or damage-related cues.
A mutation that changes a receptor’s ligand-binding, membrane, or intracellular signaling domain can alter whether and how the pathway responds.
Mutations in intracellular signaling components can change propagation, amplification, termination, or output even when ligand binding is normal.
A chemical that binds or modifies a signaling-pathway component can increase or decrease pathway activity depending on its interaction.
A defective phosphatase can prolong or alter phosphorylation states of pathway proteins; the effect depends on whether those phosphorylated targets are active or inactive.
Homeostasis is dynamic regulation of internal conditions within ranges compatible with function despite internal and external change.
A set point is a regulated target value or range used by a feedback system; set points can vary with physiological context.
A feedback loop is a regulatory pathway in which a system’s output or response influences the process that generated it.
A stimulus is a change in a regulated variable or condition that can be detected by a feedback system.
A sensor detects a relevant change and generates information used by the regulatory system; sensors may be molecular, cellular, or organismal.
A feedback system compares or integrates incoming information and coordinates downstream responses; this role need not be a brain or nervous-system center.
An effector is a component whose activity changes the regulated variable or system output.
The response is the system change produced by effectors; in negative feedback it opposes the initial deviation, while in positive feedback it reinforces the ongoing change.
Sweating and shivering can participate in negative-feedback regulation of body temperature by promoting heat loss or heat production/conservation.
Insulin and glucagon participate in negative-feedback regulation of blood glucose by promoting opposing physiological responses when glucose deviates from regulated ranges.
During labor, cervical stretch can promote oxytocin release, which strengthens uterine contractions and increases cervical stretch until delivery terminates the loop.
Blood clotting can involve positive-feedback amplification in which activated platelets and clotting factors recruit or activate additional components until the breach is sealed.
Ethylene can promote fruit-ripening processes that stimulate additional ethylene production, creating positive-feedback amplification in many fruits.
Disrupted regulatory mechanisms can contribute to disease, including dysregulated glucose control or cell proliferation, but disease is not defined solely as loss of homeostasis.
In multicellular organisms, signaling pathways coordinate cell activities that help regulate organismal internal conditions.
A genome is the complete set of genetic material in a cell or organism.
Histones are DNA-associated proteins around which eukaryotic DNA is wrapped as part of chromatin organization.
A nucleosome consists of DNA wrapped around a core of histone proteins and is a fundamental unit of eukaryotic chromatin.
Chromatin is the DNA-protein complex that constitutes eukaryotic chromosomes; its compaction changes through the cell cycle.
A chromosome is a DNA molecule with associated proteins carrying genetic information; it exists throughout the cell cycle and becomes highly condensed during mitosis.
After S phase, one replicated chromosome consists of two sister chromatids produced by DNA replication.
Sister chromatids are the two replicated DNA-protein copies of a chromosome held together until they separate during anaphase.
The centromere is the specialized chromosome region that helps hold sister chromatids together and organizes kinetochore assembly.
A kinetochore is a protein complex assembled at the centromere of each chromatid where spindle microtubules attach.
Many prokaryotes have a main circular chromosome in the nucleoid, but chromosome number and topology vary among species.
Eukaryotic nuclear genomes are organized into one or more linear chromosomes.
Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding gene loci and similar structural organization but can contain different alleles; they are distinct from sister chromatids.
A somatic cell is a non-gamete body cell; in a diploid organism most somatic cells carry two homologous chromosome sets.
Diploid (2n) describes cells with two chromosome sets, one set inherited from each biological parent in sexually reproducing diploid organisms.
A gamete is a haploid reproductive cell produced through meiosis or meiotic processes, not a cell that itself divides by meiosis.
Haploid (n) describes a cell with one chromosome set.
Interphase comprises G1, S, and G2 and is commonly the longest portion of the cell cycle, although duration varies widely.
M phase includes mitosis and usually cytokinesis, coordinating nuclear chromosome segregation with cell division.
The mitotic spindle is a microtubule-based apparatus that organizes and segregates chromosomes during mitosis.
In animal cells, centrosomes organize spindle microtubules and move apart as the mitotic spindle forms.
Prometaphase is the mitotic interval in which the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle microtubules gain access to and attach to kinetochores.
The metaphase plate is an imaginary plane at the cell equator where chromosomes align during metaphase.
A cleavage furrow is the inward constriction of an animal cell membrane during cytokinesis, driven by a contractile ring.
The animal-cell contractile ring is composed mainly of actin filaments with myosin motors and constricts the cell during cytokinesis.
In plant cytokinesis, Golgi-derived vesicles fuse near the center of the cell to form a cell plate that develops into new cell wall and membranes between daughter cells.
DNA replication doubles DNA content and chromatid number but does not double chromosome number when chromosomes are counted by centromeres.
When sister chromatids separate at anaphase, each former chromatid becomes an individual daughter chromosome; chromosome count transiently doubles within the still-undivided cell.
Mitotic stages can be identified from chromosome condensation, alignment, separation, nuclear-envelope state, and cytokinesis features in micrographs.
Chromosome movement during anaphase depends on kinetochore microtubule dynamics and spindle forces; microtubule shortening is an important contributor but not the sole spindle process.
Eukaryotic chromatin consists primarily of DNA associated with proteins, especially histones.
For a diploid organism, if gametes contain n chromosomes, typical somatic cells contain 2n chromosomes.
Failure of sister-chromatid segregation can produce daughter cells with unequal chromosome numbers.
A cell-cycle checkpoint is a regulatory control point where internal and external information influences whether the cell proceeds, pauses, exits, repairs damage, or initiates another response.
At the G1 checkpoint, cell growth conditions, signaling cues, and DNA integrity influence commitment to continue through the division cycle or enter/maintain a nondividing state.
G0 is a nondividing state outside the active division cycle; some cells can reenter the cycle, while many terminally differentiated cells remain nondividing for long periods.
The G2 checkpoint helps prevent entry into mitosis when DNA replication is incomplete or DNA damage remains unresolved.
The spindle assembly checkpoint delays anaphase until chromosomes have appropriate kinetochore-microtubule attachment and alignment.
Cell-cycle arrest is a pause in progression that can provide time for repair or prevent segregation/division under unsuitable conditions.
DNA damage can activate checkpoint pathways that promote repair, cell-cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis depending on context.
Apoptosis is regulated programmed cell death that can remove damaged, unnecessary, or potentially dangerous cells.
Cyclins are regulatory proteins whose concentrations often rise and fall during the cell cycle and whose binding helps activate cyclin-dependent kinases.
A cyclin-dependent kinase is a protein kinase whose activity depends on regulatory interactions including cyclin binding.
An active cyclin-CDK complex phosphorylates target proteins that promote or regulate specific cell-cycle events.
Students should understand that cyclin-CDK interactions regulate the cell cycle, but memorization of specific cyclin-CDK pairs is beyond current AP Exam scope.
Growth-factor signaling can influence cell-cycle progression, but memorization of specific growth factors is beyond current AP Exam scope.
Growth factors can activate signal-transduction pathways that influence cyclin/CDK activity and cell-cycle progression.
Many normal animal cells reduce proliferation when cell density/contact signals indicate crowded conditions; this is commonly called density-dependent inhibition.
Many normal animal cells require attachment to extracellular matrix or an appropriate substrate to proliferate; loss of anchorage dependence can accompany transformation.
Cancer is a disease of dysregulated cell behavior in which genetic/epigenetic changes enable uncontrolled proliferation and other malignant properties.
Cancer develops through accumulation of alterations that affect genes controlling proliferation, genome maintenance, cell death, and related processes; there is no universal fixed mutation count.
Cancer cells can acquire changes that let them bypass normal cell-cycle checkpoints and continue dividing despite signals that would arrest normal cells.
Cancer cells can acquire changes that reduce normal apoptosis responses and allow survival despite serious cellular abnormalities.
Many transformed/cancer cell populations acquire mechanisms that support very extensive or indefinite proliferation in culture, but this is not a literal property of every individual cancer cell.
A tumor is a mass of abnormally proliferating cells; tumors may be benign or malignant.
A benign tumor is a nonmalignant localized mass whose cells do not invade surrounding tissue or metastasize; benign does not mean “cancerous later.”
A malignant tumor contains cancer cells capable of invasive growth and potentially spread to distant sites.
Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from a primary tumor to distant sites where secondary tumors may form.
Ultraviolet radiation can damage DNA and increase skin-cancer risk; reducing excessive UV exposure and using appropriate sun protection can reduce risk.
Tobacco smoke contains carcinogens that cause DNA damage and increase cancer risk; nicotine is primarily the addictive agent and should not be taught as the main mutagenic carcinogen.
Do not encode “drink water” or generic avoidance of fatty foods as direct mechanistic cancer-prevention rules; preserve only evidence-supported risk-reduction guidance.
Vinblastine binds tubulin and inhibits microtubule assembly, disrupting spindle formation/kinetochore attachment and activating mitotic arrest before normal anaphase progression.
Given a biological scenario, distinguish direct-contact, local, synaptic/paracrine, and long-distance signaling using distance, medium, and receptor context.
Infer how a change in receptor binding-site structure changes ligand specificity or pathway activation.
Map an unfamiliar pathway diagram to reception, transduction, and response and justify each step.
Predict downstream effects of a receptor/pathway mutation or chemical inhibitor using causal pathway logic.
